title: De Beque Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: De Beque wells have a 63 ft median depth, but records range to 1,350 ft. See yields, water levels, costs and local risks.
h1: What De Beque Wells Are Really Like
intro_html:
Buying land in De Beque means looking past the permit map and asking what the local wells actually produce. Within 5 miles of town, Colorado Division of Water Resources records show 136 permitted wells, with 51 recorded as constructed. Reported depths are often shallow, but the local range is wide. Most permits use an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer, so conditions can change quickly from one parcel to the next.

This page uses the available permit records to explain likely depth, yield, water levels, drilling cost and the checks that matter before buying or building. The records are useful for setting expectations, not for guaranteeing a result on a specific lot.

sections.heading: De Beque Well Depth Depends on the Ground Below the Lot
sections.html:
The median reported well depth near De Beque is 63 feet, and the middle half runs from 48 to 106 feet. That makes a shallow well a reasonable starting assumption for a drilling estimate, but not a safe promise. Seventy-one percent of reported wells are under 100 feet, while 19% fall between 300 and 600 feet. The deepest record reaches 1,350 feet.

For a buyer, the spread matters more than the median. A driller bidding a 63-foot hole may be close for one alluvial location and far off for a parcel in more difficult fractured ground. Ask for nearby completed well logs, casing and grout details, and a written explanation of what happens if the first target does not produce.

sections.heading: Reported De Beque Yields Are Strong, but the Sample Is Small
sections.html:
Among the 18 wells with a reported pump yield, the median is 15.0 gallons per minute. The middle half is 13.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute, and 61% of reported wells produce more than 15 gallons per minute. Another 33% fall between 5 and 15 gallons per minute. Six percent are in the 1-to-5-gallon range, and none of the reported wells are under 1 gallon per minute.

Those figures are encouraging for household planning, but only 18 records include yield information. A permit map is not a test of your parcel. Confirm the expected yield with the driller and plan storage around the well's actual production. An exempt household-use well also has a 35-gallon-per-minute pumping limit, regardless of a higher reported capacity.

sections.heading: De Beque Water Levels Look Shallow in the Available Records
sections.html:
Only 8 wells report a static water level, so the water-level sample is limited. The median depth to water is 9 feet, with the middle half between 6 and 12 feet. That suggests shallow groundwater in the wells with measurements, which can reduce pumping lift and affect excavation planning.

The permit history does not provide a complete water-level-by-decade series, so it cannot establish a reliable trend of a dropping or rising water table. Do not treat the shallow median as a guarantee for an untested lot. Seasonal conditions, well construction and the local aquifer can all affect the measurement. A driller should verify water level during construction and explain how it affects pump placement and protection from surface water.

sections.heading: De Beque Permit History Shows Long-Term Drilling Activity
sections.html:
Permit activity is spread across several decades, with the largest group in the 2000s: 43 permits. The records include 27 permits from the 2010s and 7 from the 2020s, with the newest permit issued in 2025. Domestic or household wells make up 51% of the use mix. Monitoring wells account for 26%, stock use 10%, and irrigation 4%.

Most recorded drilling is associated with Shelton Drilling Corporation, listed on 47 wells. Authorized, identified as Pe, Pg, appears on 10, and Steve Shelton Drilling, Inc., identified as Shelton, Steve, appears on 3. A permit name is not a recommendation or a current availability check. Use the records to identify local experience, then verify licensing, insurance, scheduling and the exact scope of the bid.

sections.heading: A De Beque Well May Cost $9,200 to $16,700 Finished
sections.html:
The local cost model assumes mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground. Typical drilling is priced at $50 to $75 per foot. At the 63-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at about $3,200 to $4,700. That is only the hole, not a usable water system.

A finished well including the pump, pressure tank, trenching and electrical is estimated at $9,200 to $16,700 at the median depth. A deeper-than-typical hole, difficult access, casing requirements or an unsuccessful first attempt can change the final bill. Ask whether the quote includes permitting, casing, grout, development, pump testing, electrical work and connection to the house. Get the depth assumption in writing so a per-foot price can be compared fairly.

sections.heading: Checks That Matter Before Building Near De Beque
sections.html:
Yield is not the only risk. The depth records range from shallow wells to a 1,350-foot record, and fractured-bedrock conditions can be unpredictable even across nearby parcels. Ask about the chance of a dry hole, the contractor's backup plan and the cost of abandoning or redrilling if the target fails.

Environmental review also belongs in the purchase decision. The mapped area within about 10 miles includes 72 PFAS sampling or contamination sites. There are no historic mine features and no EPA Superfund or cleanup sites in the supplied records, but that does not replace a property-specific water test. Check the well location, septic setbacks, drainfield area, access for a rig, and room for a pressure tank and utilities before finalizing a building site. Confirm water rights, permit conditions and any augmentation requirement with Colorado DWR, especially where water use is legally constrained.

sections.heading: Use Nearby Wells Before Choosing a De Beque Lot
sections.html:
Start with the well permits closest to the parcel, then compare their depths, aquifer descriptions, construction details and reported yields. The broader records around De Beque can provide context, but a nearby log is more useful than a regional average. Look at properties toward Parachute and Mesa as well as the immediate area, while remembering that distance does not make ground conditions identical. Collbran, Battlement Mesa, Palisade and Fruitvale are also nearby reference areas in the broader map.

Before closing, make the well investigation a written contingency when possible. Have a Colorado driller review the logs, inspect access and price the complete system rather than just drilling. If you are building, reserve the well, septic and driveway areas together. A lot can have adequate water and still be difficult or expensive because the well pad, septic field and house cannot be arranged safely.

faq.q: How deep are wells in De Beque?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within 5 miles of De Beque is 63 feet, and the middle half runs from 48 to 106 feet. Seventy-one percent are under 100 feet. Conditions vary sharply, though: 19% are 300 to 600 feet deep, and the deepest record is 1,350 feet. Nearby logs are more useful than the median alone.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in De Beque?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $50 to $75 per foot in mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground. At the 63-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $3,200 to $4,700. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is estimated at $9,200 to $16,700. Deeper drilling or difficult access can increase the total.

faq.q: How much water do De Beque wells produce?
faq.a: Only 18 wells report a pump yield, but the reported median is 15.0 gallons per minute. The middle half is 13.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute, and 61% of reported wells exceed 15 gallons per minute. These figures do not guarantee a new well. Have the driller test the completed well and size storage to its actual production.

faq.q: Is well water safe in De Beque?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from a permit map. The mapped area within about 10 miles contains 72 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, so a property-specific laboratory test is important. Ask for the well construction record, test for relevant contaminants, and retest after construction or changes nearby. The records show no EPA Superfund or cleanup sites and no historic mine features.

faq.q: Are De Beque wells connected to the Denver Basin aquifer?
faq.a: No wells in the supplied records are identified as Denver Basin aquifer wells. One hundred thirty-four are associated with an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer. That description does not guarantee a consistent result: fractured rock can vary across short distances. Have a driller review nearby logs and confirm the expected aquifer, depth, casing and grout approach before you buy or build.
